claims.text: A covariance matrix of atomic displacements can be used to extract effective vibrational frequencies and vibrational entropy.
Including displacement covariances corrects the entropy overestimation produced by treating atomic displacements independently.
Eigenvalues of the displacement covariance matrix can yield an effective vibrational density of states for quantum entropy evaluation.
The covariance-derived effective frequencies incorporate some anharmonicity.
The covariance approach captures electron–vibration interactions relevant to fusion free energies.
The covariance method is applicable to both solid and fluid states.
A short, statistically converged simulation is sufficient to replace long AIMD or TOR-TILD free-energy trajectories.
Configurational ensembles rather than time evolution itself are sufficient for estimating covariance-based vibrational entropy.
The covariance method agrees well with experimental vibrational entropies for BCC sodium and FCC aluminum.
Prior results support the covariance method in binary systems.
The method should extend to moderately complex high-entropy alloys when displacement statistics remain approximately Gaussian.
The method should be less accurate under extreme anharmonicity or strongly non-Gaussian displacement distributions.
The covariance method will predict high-temperature free energies and fusion temperatures within approximately 10% of full AIMD or TOR-TILD results.
The covariance method will provide a computational speed-up of 10–100 times over full AIMD or TOR-TILD workflows.
Accurate vibrational entropy from displacement covariance is sufficient to maintain fidelity in total solid and liquid phase free energies.
The covariance matrix encapsulates effective vibrational modes and effective force constants.
Vibrational density of states can serve as a diagnostic for whether atomic displacement statistics are significantly non-Gaussian.
FCC aluminum is an example of a binary metal system.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field distinguishes elemental and binary systems and lists FCC Al among the examples, whereas the experiment design explicitly calls FCC Al a binary metal system. Pure aluminum is elemental, not binary.
